### R-292 | area: chat-platform-limits | parallel-safe: no | automatable: no

**Summary:** A genuine Vercel-platform 413 is the one thing nothing below the platform can produce — `next dev` enforces no such cap, and the App Router's 4.5 MB body limit is generated by the platform before the route handler ever runs, with no configuration knob for it. Confirm the client-side attach-time refusal fires on a real deploy, and record the actually-observed response shape, since that is the only proof the status-keyed classifier in R-284 matches what Vercel really sends.

**BLOCKED AS WRITTEN — step 3 is not performable from the app's own UI, and step 4 depends on it.** Steps 1, 2 and 4 stay runnable *if* step 3 is replaced by the direct-request procedure below; without that, step 4 has nothing to record and this case cannot be satisfied. Recorded rather than quietly left as an instruction nobody can follow.

**Steps:**
1. Deploy the app to Vercel (not a local `next dev` server).
2. With a résumé loaded, attach **a PDF or image of at least 3,500,000 bytes (3.5 MB decimal / 3.34 MiB — pick a file that is unambiguously over the gate under BOTH readings)** and attempt to attach it. Confirm the attach-time refusal names the file and quotes `"2.8 MB"` (`MAX_ATTACHMENT_SIZE_LABEL`). *(Do NOT use "roughly 3 MB": the gate is `file.size > 3_000_000` bytes, strictly greater, so a file macOS reports as "3.0 MB" can be exactly 3,000,000 bytes, be **accepted**, and read as a false failure of this step.)*
3. **There is no attachment or combination that passes the client's gates and still reaches the platform's cap — the step this case used to ask for does not exist.** Three gates stack, all below Vercel's 4.5 MB: the per-file gate in `addChatAttachments` refuses a non-`.docx` above 3,000,000 bytes (`if (!isDocx && file.size > MAX_BINARY_ATTACHMENT_BYTES)`, `chatbot.js`); the aggregate gate in the same loop refuses once the running attachment payload would exceed `MAX_ATTACHMENT_PAYLOAD_BYTES` = 4,000,000 (`if (runningTotal + cost > MAX_ATTACHMENT_PAYLOAD_BYTES)`); and `runChatRequest` measures the whole serialized body (`const bodyBytes = new TextEncoder().encode(requestBody).length`) and throws above `MAX_REQUEST_BYTES` = 4,500,000 **before `fetch` is ever called** (`if (bodyBytes > MAX_REQUEST_BYTES) { refusedBeforeSend = true; throw new Error(buildRefusal(true)); }`). *(Anchors converted to symbols — see R-284 step 1; the four line numbers previously here were all stale. The gates themselves, and the arithmetic, are unchanged — see R-293 below for what DID change in the message these gates produce.)* Provoking a genuine platform 413 therefore requires **bypassing the client entirely** — issuing a direct `POST` to the deployed `/api/chat` endpoint with a body over 4.5 MB (curl, Postman, or a devtools console `fetch`), which is what this step must say and previously did not. Do that, then open the response.
4. Record VERBATIM — in this entry's next amendment — the response's HTTP status code and its `content-type` header value, or explicitly note that no `content-type` header was present. Note also that the body came from a hand-issued request, not from the app.

**Expected:** Step 2's refusal fires client-side **at ATTACH time**, inside `addChatAttachments`, before the file ever enters the tray. **It is NOT true that "the request never reaches the network"** — the earlier Expected said so and it is wrong for step 2 as written: nothing is sent at attach time because nothing is being sent at all, and a message the user types and sends *afterwards* is an ordinary, un-attached request that reaches the network and succeeds normally. The correct claim is narrower: the refused file never becomes part of any request. Step 4's recorded status and content-type are the only real-world evidence that `readChatResponse`'s status-only classification actually matches what Vercel sends for an oversized request on this platform and account — nobody in this repo has recorded that observed value yet, so this case is not satisfied by a green automated suite alone, and as of this amendment it is **not satisfied at all**.

### R-293 | area: chat-platform-limits | parallel-safe: yes | automatable: no

**Summary:** A user with a large amount of tracked application history and ZERO attachments can still 413, because `applicationsContext` serializes every tracked application's full job description and tailored résumé, unbounded, on every send. The failure message must name that real cause, not attachments — and client-side trimming was deliberately NOT implemented, for a reason that must not be "fixed" by a future change adding it back in.

**FIXTURE DISCIPLINE — read before quoting any number below.** Every figure in this case is fixture-sensitive, and the ORIGINAL version of this entry was wrong for exactly that reason: it told testers 200 applications would be refused, when in reality they sent fine. The numbers were then re-stated from a fixture family with **no `applicationUrl` and no `stages`** — a shape no real tracked application has — and were wrong again. Each number below therefore names its fixture. The two families are:
- **TEST fixture** — `bulkApplications` in `lib/chat/chatbot.request.test.js`: no `applicationUrl`, no `stages`, the first 25 carrying 20,000-character documents and the rest bare. Marginal cost **168 bytes/application** past the slice.
- **REALISTIC fixture** — a real tracked application: a real job-board `applicationUrl` with query string, two interview stages, an accented ~4,500-character posting and an accented ~6,000-character tailored résumé. Marginal cost **483 bytes/application** past the slice.

**Steps:**
1. With an account carrying roughly 200 tracked applications and NO attachments in the chat tray, send a message. **The send must SUCCEED.** Note carefully what this step does and does not prove — see the Expected. **No documented way to reach this account state exists, and the repo ships no seeding tool**; the step is performable only by someone who already has such an account, or who builds a seeder first. Recorded honestly rather than left as a step nobody can run.
2. **Press `Clear` first, so this runs in a NEW thread. Then switch the engine control to "Embedded (no AI)"**, and ask "how many applications do I have?" Confirm the count is the true total, not 25.
   - *Why the engine must be named:* the Gemini path's renderer only ever sees the first 25 applications, by design, and `DEFAULT_ENGINE` is `"gemini"` (`app/settings/engine.js:31`) — asking on the default engine would report 25 and read as a false regression.
   - *Why the new thread must be named, and this is a second, distinct trap this case previously walked testers straight into:* `countPriorIntent` (`hello-world/lib/chat/localAssistant.js:431-437`) counts prior user turns of the same intent and passes the result as `depth`. At `depth ≥ 1`, `summarizeApplications` returns a per-application breakdown — `Here's each one: … and 190 more.` — **with no total in it at all.** Asking on Gemini, switching engines, and re-asking in the same thread lands exactly there and looks like a failure of this step. `Clear` resets the transcript and therefore the depth.
3. To reach the refusal this case originally described, read the message the user sees at that scale. The scale is **order 10³, not 10⁴** on any realistic account — see the Expected for the three measured thresholds. As with step 1, **there is no documented way to reach such an account state and no seeding tool in the repo**; in practice this step is verified against the harness, not a live account, and it is recorded here so the claim in the Expected is attributable.

**Expected:** Step 1's fixture now SENDS — but state precisely what that does and does not demonstrate, because the earlier version of this entry overstated it in both directions:

- **Pre-fix (unbounded) at 200 applications: 2,730,835 bytes = 2.73 MB on the REALISTIC fixture — UNDER the 4,500,000-byte cap.** It would **not** have been refused. The earlier "measured 8.0 MB" was never a realistic-account measurement: **8.12 MB** is what 200 applications cost unbounded when each carries the TEST fixture's inflated 20,000 + 20,000-character documents. Both figures are real; only the second one describes a real user.
- **Bounded at 200 applications: 206,435 bytes = 201.6 KB on the REALISTIC fixture.** The earlier "roughly 120 KB" is the **TEST** fixture's figure — 120,615 bytes = 117.8 KB — not a realistic-account one.
- So the honest statement of the win at 200 applications is a fall from **2.73 MB to 201.6 KB** — a 13× reduction that keeps a large-history account comfortably clear of the cap, rather than a rescue from a refusal that, on a realistic fixture at this size, was never happening.

`applicationsContext` no longer serializes every tracked application's full job description and tailored résumé unbounded — `lib/chat/applicationContext.js`'s `projectApplicationsForRequest` bounds those two fields for the first `MAX_APPLICATIONS` (25) applications and drops them past that, the same slice the Gemini renderer already used.

Step 2's embedded-engine count, **asked in a fresh thread**, is the TRUE total application count, never 25: the 25-application cap applies only to what the Gemini renderer shows, and the embedded path (`lib/chat/localAssistant.js`) never goes through that renderer.

Step 3's threshold is **order 10³ for any realistic account**, not the order 10⁴ this entry previously claimed. Measured, three fixtures, binary-searched against the client-side `MAX_REQUEST_BYTES` gate:

| Fixture | Marginal cost | Crosses 4,500,000 bytes at |
|---|---|---|
| TEST (`bulkApplications`, no URL, no stages) | 168 B/app | **26,086** applications |
| REALISTIC (real URL, 2 stages) | 483 B/app | **9,004** applications |
| REALISTIC with a full four-stage interview loop | 701 B/app | **5,838** applications |

The previously stated "order 10⁴ … measured 26,086" is the TEST-fixture row only, and it is the least representative of the three. At that scale the message still names saved application history as the cause — NOT "remove an attachment", which remains impossible advice with an empty tray.

**AC-50: what decides that message changed shape entirely under chunk A2, and this entry's constant names were stale against it.** Before A2 this was a straight binary choice between two constants, keyed only on "is the attachment tray empty" — `TOO_BIG_NO_ATTACHMENTS_MESSAGE` (`chatbot.js:131-135` as of this writing before A2) for an empty tray, `TOO_BIG_MESSAGE` (`:120-122`) otherwise, and the earlier anchor `:121-125` for the former landed on the latter — the exact wording this case says must NOT appear. **A2 replaced that pair with a five-way selection among `export const` primaries, chosen by which of five WIRE BODY SECTIONS (`attachedFiles`, `pinnedContext`, `messages`, `resumeText`, `applications`, in that fixed, exported `BODY_SECTION_ORDER`) is measurably the largest contributor to the oversized request, plus a sixth message for the case where removing even the largest section still would not bring the body under the cap** (`refusalMessageFor`, and the constants themselves, in **`hello-world/lib/chat/refusal.js`** — `chatbot.js` re-exports every one of those names, so an import written against `chatbot.js` still resolves). *(Both anchors here cited `lib/chat/chatbot.js` line ranges for code that **left that file**: A2's extraction moved the whole vocabulary and its selection functions to `refusal.js`. Repointed to the file that actually holds them, by symbol.)*

For R-293's own fixture family — bulk applications, empty attachment tray, no pinned context, no résumé uploaded — `applications` is overwhelmingly the largest of the five sections, so the constant the measured selection picks is **exactly the same one this case always exercised**, now named `TOO_BIG_APPLICATIONS_MESSAGE` (`hello-world/lib/chat/refusal.js`, re-exported from `chatbot.js`): *"That message is too large to send (the platform limit is 4.5 MB total) — most of it is your saved application history, which every message carries. Nothing in this panel can shrink it; removing applications you no longer track is what reduces it."* **This case's substantive expectation is unchanged — the fixture still refuses, and the message still names application history, never attachments, as the cause.** Only the mechanism (measured selection instead of a tray-emptiness check) and the constant's name changed.

The deleted `TOO_BIG_NO_ATTACHMENTS_MESSAGE` carried, in addition to naming the cause, the closing clause *"Try asking about one specific company or role, or send a shorter, smaller message, and try again."* **That clause is gone, deliberately, and must not be restored as a "lost" message (AC-26).** `applicationsContext` (the `const applicationsContext = projectApplicationsForRequest(mappedApplications)` line inside `runChatRequest`, `lib/chat/chatbot.js`) never reads the user's typed question — it serializes the tracked application history independently of what was asked — so narrowing the question could never have reduced the body by one byte. It was impossible advice standing next to correct advice, and A2 removed it everywhere in the file (swept, comments included, by `lib/chat/chatbot.refusal.test.js`'s AC-26 suite).

**The previous Expected's closing clause is now OBSOLETE ON EVIDENCE, not stepped over — recorded here rather than silently deleted.** It read: "Do not add client-side trimming without first giving the embedded assistant's context builder a capped, prioritized view of applications; adding naive trimming against today's unbounded consumer would trade this message for a different, silent data-loss bug." The shipped bound gives every consumer an UNCAPPED, UNPRIORITIZED, COMPLETE view of applications — strictly stronger than what that clause asked for — because it drops no application, no scheduled date and no stage name/type/outcome: only `jobDescription` and `tailoredResume`, which `lib/chat/localAssistant.js` reads nowhere, are bounded per application. Two fields ARE dropped outright — `stages[].interviewers` and `stages[].notes` — and neither consumer of `body.applications` reads either one (`app/api/chat/route.js`'s renderer stops at `outcome`; `lib/chat/localAssistant.js` reads only `scheduledAt`/`name`/`type`). They still reach the model by a different route: `buildApplicationContextString` / `buildStageContextString` in `hello-world/lib/chat/chatbot.js` render raw Supabase rows into `pinnedContext`, a different body field this projection never touches. The named harm ("a scheduled interview vanishing") is now structurally impossible, guarded directly by the `[L3]` embedded-assistant equality in `lib/chat/applicationContext.test.js` and by `app/api/chat/route.js`'s embedded branch at `:185-198`, which still hands `localChatReply` the full, unsliced applications array.

### R-295 | area: chat-platform-limits | parallel-safe: yes | automatable: no

**Summary:** `MAX_APPLICATIONS`, `MAX_JD_CHARS` and `MAX_TAILORED_CHARS` (`hello-world/lib/chat/applicationContext.js`) are a DEPLOY CONTRACT, not local tunables: both the client-side projection and the server-side renderer read them, so RAISING any of the three requires a coordinated server-then-client release. **No single-tree test can catch a violation** — a test imports each constant once and applies that one value to both sides in the same run, so raising a number moves both sides of the test together and the skew never appears. This case exists because the only instrument that can see the hazard is a human reading a diff before it ships.

**Steps:**
1. This case is triggered by a CHANGE, not run on a schedule. It applies to **four** kinds of diff, not one:
   - **RAISING** any of `MAX_APPLICATIONS` (25), `MAX_JD_CHARS` (1500) or `MAX_TAILORED_CHARS` (2000).
   - **LOWERING `MAX_APPLICATIONS`** — and, just as much, **ROLLING BACK** such a lowering. Lowering that constant is NOT safe; the earlier text here said it was, and that was wrong. See the Expected below for the measurement.
   - **Adding a field to `renderApplicationsSection`** (`hello-world/lib/chat/applicationContext.js`) that `projectApplicationsForRequest`'s allowlist in the same file does not also carry. The allowlist is on the identical two-sided contract as the three numbers, and this trigger fires with **no constant changed at all**. The live example is this very change, which dropped `stages[].interviewers` and `stages[].notes` from the projection: re-adding either one to the renderer later, without also adding it to the allowlist, produces the same silent skew and fires none of the other triggers.
   - Correspondingly, **removing a field from the allowlist** that the renderer still reads.
   **Lowering `MAX_JD_CHARS` or `MAX_TAILORED_CHARS` is the one genuinely safe move on this list** — an old client pre-slices to the larger old `max + 1`, so the new server's `truncate` still sees a string over its own smaller `max`, re-cuts it and appends the ellipsis itself. For every other change above, **do not skip steps 2-4.**
2. Read the DEPLOY CONTRACT comment above the three constants in `hello-world/lib/chat/applicationContext.js` and confirm the diff's author acknowledged the two-sided release rather than treating the number (or the allowlist) as local.
3. Confirm the release plan ships the SERVER change first and then either cache-busts the client bundle or waits out the window in which browsers can still be running the previous JS, before anything relies on the new bound. For a **lowering** of `MAX_APPLICATIONS`, confirm the plan also covers the rollback path, since that is the direction that loses data.
4. After the deploy, hard-reload a browser tab (or open a private window) before checking that the new bound took effect. A tab left open across the deploy is running the OLD projection and will show the OLD behaviour — that is the hazard, not a bug in the deploy. **State the observable plainly, because the obvious guess is wrong: nothing in the UI renders the applications block.** It is built server-side inside `renderApplicationsSection` and goes straight into the model's `systemInstruction`; it is never returned to the client and never appears in devtools' response. The only thing a human can observe end to end is **the model's answer quality** — ask the assistant something that can only be answered from the job description or tailored résumé of an application in the 26-50 range (e.g. "what does the posting for *<company #40>* say about on-call?") and see whether it can answer at all. If you need a harder observable than that, read the *request* body in devtools instead (`POST /api/chat` → Payload → `applications`) and count how many entries carry a non-null `jobDescription` — that is the client half of the skew, directly visible, and it is the half that goes wrong.

**Expected:** With a skewed client and server, the failure is SILENT and no error appears anywhere.

- **`MAX_JD_CHARS` / `MAX_TAILORED_CHARS`, RAISED:** the old client pre-slices to the old `max + 1`, the new server's `truncate` sees a string already under its larger `max`, and the text passes through un-ellipsised — the model reads less of the posting or résumé than the new server believes it configured.
- **`MAX_APPLICATIONS`, RAISED 25 → 50 against a client still pinned at 25:** worse and harder to notice — 25 whole `Job Description:` lines and 25 `Tailored Resume:` lines vanish, while applications 26-50 still render their header, company, role, status and interview stages, so the block LOOKS complete and nothing is missing to count. **88,550 characters** is the figure to expect, but it is the **arithmetic ceiling, not a typical measurement**: it equals exactly `25 × ((19 + 1501 + 1) + (19 + 2001 + 1))` — the two label prefixes are 19 characters each, `truncate` emits `max` characters plus the `…`, and each line carries a newline — and it is reached only when **all 25** dropped applications carry BOTH an over-cap job description and an over-cap tailored résumé. The **percentage does not have a single value**, which is why the earlier "49%" here did not reproduce: it is **45.8%** on a *realistic* fixture (real `applicationUrl`, two interview stages, ~4.5k-character posting, ~6k-character tailored résumé — intended block 193,500 characters) and **48.7%** on a *lean* fixture with no `applicationUrl` and no stages (intended block 181,847 characters). Quote the fixture whenever you quote the percentage.
- **`MAX_APPLICATIONS`, LOWERED — and this is the case the earlier text told you to skip:** the damage is symmetric, and the direction that bites is a NEW client against an OLD server. That is exactly the state after **rolling back** a 25 → 10 lowering, and also the state while stale new-bundle tabs persist after such a rollback. Measured, a client projecting at 10 against a server rendering at 25: **53,130 characters lost, 58.5% of the block**, with **all 25** applications still rendering their headers, so nothing appears missing. Unlike the two character caps, there is no server-side remedy — the client sends `null`, and `truncate` cannot re-cut a field that never arrived.
- **Allowlist skew (no constant changed):** a field added to `renderApplicationsSection` but absent from `projectApplicationsForRequest`'s allowlist simply renders as nothing, on every request from every client, old or new. This one is not even a deploy-window hazard — it is permanent until the allowlist catches up.

A green test suite is not evidence that any of these landed correctly; only a hard-reloaded client against the new server is.

**Known flakes, unrelated to this change:** `app/hooks/useDriveDocuments.connect.test.js`'s *"Overwrite retries with onConflict exactly 'overwrite'"* and *"Save as a new Doc retries with onConflict exactly 'new'"* (both recorded in R-282) fail only under full-suite load and pass in isolation — each is a promise deliberately left outside `act()`. Neither is touched by, nor caused by, the chat fix recorded in R-284 through R-294.
